source.title: Adversarial Attacks on the Interpretation of Neuron Activation Maximization
source.authors: Géraldin Nanfack; A. Fulleringer; Jonathan Marty; Michael Eickenberg; Eugene Belilovsky

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses top-k neuron visualizations as the target of adversarial attacks and reports attack performance. It does not measure the natural share of interpretable neuron poles, explanation accuracy on held-out activations, automated explanation scores, or the other specified claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported attacks intentionally fine-tune models to change feature visualizations, so their outcomes are not evidence about how often unmodified models have interpretable neurons. The paper's cited findings are not recorded as study results. Detailed attack examples and the fairwashing results do not test any listed claim version; accuracy and whack-a-mole metrics are not included as rows because they do not measure the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes pretrained CNNs (AlexNet, EfficientNet) on purpose to change neurons' top-k visualizations, then reports how well the attack works. It never measures, in unmodified models, the share of interpretable neurons. It also does not test whether activating-example explanations predict held-out firing, or score explanations automatically. Its finding that top-k images can misrepresent a channel arises only under deliberate manipulation, so it does not test V6 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also say the results cast doubt on using top-k feature visualization to build complete mechanistic interpretations. They report little evidence that the attacks merely move a feature to another channel (whack-a-mole), while noting their metrics for this may be imperfect.
record.recipe_differences: The study adversarially fine-tunes pretrained CNNs to alter activation-maximization visualizations; it does not perform the Qwen neuron-pole audit or the other methods in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with layer depth: the earliest AlexNet layers are harder to modify than later layers. The study also reports separate push-down and push-up attacks and an EfficientNet layer ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial fine-tuning replaces neurons' top-k natural images with small accuracy loss (<0.5%). Conv4–Conv5 change more than Conv1–Conv2: CLIP-δ 0.205–0.249 vs 0.043–0.056. EfficientNet CLIP-δ is 0.262.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-k activating-image interpretations of CNN neurons can be deliberately altered without changing model outputs, more easily in later layers.

fits_no_version.finding: After attack, activation rankings over a large image set stay moderately correlated with the originals (Kendall-τ 0.50–0.68), even when top-k images are fully replaced or filled with decoy goldfish.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-k images can misrepresent a channel whose overall activation ordering is largely preserved.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic activation-maximizing images are largely unchanged after top-k push-down and push-up attacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Natural-image top-k visualizations and synthetic feature visualizations can be decorrelated by model manipulation.

record.problems: The attacks are intentionally induced and therefore do not estimate the prevalence of interpretable or uninterpretable neurons in unmodified models. Most visualization-change metrics are aggregates over channels; the paper notes that its whack-a-mole metrics may be imperfect. Several qualitative channel examples are visual-only.
record.rows_left_out: Individual channel visual examples and the fairwashing experiment are not itemized because they concern attack examples or fairness visualization rather than a listed claim version. Table 1 accuracy and whack-a-mole metrics are also omitted because they do not measure the listed versions' neuron-job or explanation claims.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and no one-job, two-job or unexplained shares.
No language models; no interpretability shares across scale or dense versus mixture-of-experts models.
InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron, pose detection and recursive generalization are not examined.
No estimate of interpretable-neuron share by tool quality, architecture or regularization. The EfficientNet run is an attack ablation, not an interpretability audit.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.

Top-k examples are shown to be decoupled from channel behaviour only after adversarial fine-tuning (Kendall-τ stays 0.50–0.68). Explanation fit to held-out firing in unmodified models is not measured.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ["none"]; their states describe attack success, not any claim version. The fairwashing results (Table 2, Figs 10–12) are deliberately induced and also bear on no version. The paper is vision-only, with no language models.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and the proportions of one-job, two-related-job, and not-yet-understood poles are not measured.
No audit of interpretability shares across language-model sizes, dense models, or mixture-of-experts models is reported.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization are not examined.
The proposed causes of messy neurons and the estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models are not evaluated.
Attribution graphs, their ability to explain behavior, and comparison to trained replacement models are not studied.

The study does not test whether explanations derived from activating examples predict firing on held-out inputs; it instead intentionally changes top-k visualizations through adversarial model fine-tuning.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations on new text is not studied.

rows.subject: PyTorch pretrained AlexNet
rows.operation_detail: Push-down fine-tuning of top-k natural-image visualizations; synthetic activation-maximizing images were then inspected.
rows.value: The synthetic optimal image was described as largely unaffected by the top-k attack.
rows.note: This is a qualitative result for several channels; the authors explicitly do not claim that synthetic visualization is more robust to an attack directed at it.
